hits.text:
Finally, we comment on the relationship between the zone-center two-magnon excitations in the Raman spectra and the giant spin gap in the RIXS spectra in Refs. [23,32]. It is apparent that these two features have nearly the same energy, but sharply distinct symmetries. A trivial explanation could be that they are two different but energetically degenerate objects that happen to be captured by Raman and RIXS in a complementary way. A less trivial possibility could be that they are indeed one and the same object, which would suggest a reconsideration of the conventional selection rules. Optical Raman selection rules are well defined based on the electric dipole approximation, which is justified in the fact that optical wavelengths are much larger than lattice constants and is further confirmed by the correct selection rules for the phonon modes. Resonant x-ray spectroscopy selection rules are less well defined because of contributions from higher order multipolar transitions in addition to the electric dipole transitions [34]. In the electric-dipole channel, the polarization of the incoming x ray rotating to a perpendicular polarization in the scattered x ray reflects time-reversal-symmetrybreaking excitations, whereas in the electric-quadrupole or higher multipole channels, such a rotation is naturally allowed even for excitations of the A 1 g symmetry, as the case for the RIXS on the spin gap of Sr 3 Ir 2 O 7 .

Having discussed helicity-resolved selection rules as a route for identifying chiral phonons, we now turn to another experimentally accessible signature: the helicity-dependent shift of Raman peak positions. In this context, the relevant observable is not only whether a phonon mode is allowed in a given polarization channel, but also whether the two opposite cross-helical channels resolve different phonon frequencies. One important example is the small but robust frequency offset between the cross-helical configurations (RL and LR) measured close to the Brillouin-zone center in noncentrosymmetric crystals. In the relevant backscattering geometry, the optical momentum transfer is directed along a crystal rotation axis; in reciprocal space this corresponds to a small phonon wave vector along the Γ -A line. Along this direction, the doubly degenerate E mode at Γ splits into two chiral branches with opposite handedness L = ± 1.
